scribe_response.text: What was a typical day like in your working life? In my working life, a typical day began at five in the morning, before the sun was properly up. Lakshmi made me strong tea with cardamom. I drank it standing at the kitchen window. By six I was in my car, driving the empty road toward the plant on the coast. The plant was a cluster of steel towers, pipes, uh and tanks that hummed all day and all night. Its purpose was to boil seawater and capture the steam, which condensed into fresh water. Every morning I began with um a walk through the whole facility, notebook in hand. I checked the pressure gauges one by one. I wrote the readings in the same blue ink. I trusted that notebook more than any computer, because it never crashed and I could smell its pages. The heat in the plant was fierce, so we wore um light cotton shirts and kept a bottle of water in every pocket. Near the brine pumps there was a, was a constant um roar, and we talked with our hands. The operators on the night shift would meet me at the control room with a short report. What happened next? They were Indian, Pakistani, Egyptian, and Filipino men, and we shared a respect for good order. At seven thirty I sat down with the shift supervisor, and we discussed any odd sounds or smells. A smell can tell you something is wrong long before a sensor does. After that I looked at um the maintenance list, and I planned uh which valves or filters needed attention. Scale was our eternal enemy, because the minerals in seawater coated the tubes like a stubborn crust. So we dosed the water with chemicals and um cleaned the tubes every few months. At ten the managers arrived, and we held a short meeting around a long table with weak um coffee. I disliked long meetings, so I kept mine to exactly twenty minutes by my wristwatch. Midday was the hardest time, when the sun on the steel made the whole place shimmer. I often ate lunch at my desk. It was a steel tin of rice and fish curry that Lakshmi had packed. The younger engineers teased me about it, and then they begged for a taste. In the afternoon I wrote reports, with a pencil first and then a um typewriter, and later a keyboard. Can you tell me more about that? Every report ended with a section uh called recommendations, which I considered the heart of the matter. At four I went out for a second round, and the light turned golden on the pipes. That was my favourite hour, when the machines seemed calm and almost friendly. Before leaving, I would sign the logbook and hand over to the evening engineer. The drive home was slow, with the sea on my left and the sky changing colours, colours. At home my sons would be doing homework on the dining table. They would show me their sums. Dinner was at eight, and Lakshmi insisted that we all ate together without the television. After dinner I played a game of chess with Arun, who took a long time over each move. Then I read the newspaper from the back page to the front, which is how a cricket lover does it. By ten I was asleep, and the next day would repeat in almost the same way. Some people might call such a life dull, but I found a deep satisfaction in its rhythm. A plant is like a body, and a good engineer learns to take its pulse every morning. I kept that uh routine for thirty-five years, and I would happily keep it again.
